prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We present the first systematic investigation of the [NeV] (14um/24um) and [SIII] (18um/33um) infrared line flux ratios, traditionally used to estimate the density of the ionized gas, in a sample of 41 Type 1 and Type 2 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) observed with the Infrared Spectrograph on board Spitzer. The majority of galaxies with both [NeV] lines detected have observed [NeV] line flux ratios consistent with or below the theoretical low density limit, based on calculations using currently available collision strengths and ignoring absorption and stimulated emission. We find that Type 2 AGNs have lower line flux ratios than Type 1 AGNs and that all of the galaxies with line flux ratios below the low density limit are Type 2 AGNs. We argue that differential infrared extinction to the [NeV] emitting region due to dust in the obscuring torus is responsible for the ratios below the low density limit and we suggest that the ratio may be a tracer of the inclination angle of the torus to our line of sight. Because the temperature of the gas, the amount of extinction, and the effect of absorption and stimulated emission on the line ratios are all unknown, we are not able to determine the electron densities associated with the [NeV] line flux ratios for the objects in our sample. We also find that the [SIII] emission from the galaxies in our sample is extended and originates primarily in star forming regions. Since the emission from low-ionization species is extended, any analysis using line flux ratios from such species obtained from slits of different sizes is invalid for most nearby galaxies.

outputs.L1: We present the first systematic investigation of the [Ne V] (14 μm/24 μm) and [S III] (18 μm/33 μm) infrared line flux ratios, which are traditionally used to estimate the density of ionized gas, in a sample of 41 Type 1 and Type 2 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) observed with the Infrared Spectrograph aboard *Spitzer*. Most galaxies in which both [Ne V] lines are detected exhibit observed [Ne V] line flux ratios that are consistent with, or below, the theoretical low-density limit, based on calculations using currently available collision strengths and neglecting absorption and stimulated emission. We find that Type 2 AGNs have lower line flux ratios than Type 1 AGNs, and that all galaxies with line flux ratios below the low-density limit are Type 2 AGNs. We argue that differential infrared extinction toward the [Ne V]-emitting region, caused by dust in the obscuring torus, is responsible for the ratios below the low-density limit, and we suggest that this ratio may serve as a tracer of the inclination angle of the torus relative to our line of sight. Because the gas temperature, the amount of extinction, and the effects of absorption and stimulated emission on the line ratios are all unknown, we cannot determine the electron densities associated with the [Ne V] line flux ratios for the objects in our sample. We also find that the [S III] emission from the galaxies in our sample is extended and originates primarily in star-forming regions. Since emission from low-ionization species is extended, any analysis using line flux ratios from such species obtained through slits of different sizes is invalid for most nearby galaxies.
outputs.L2:
We report the first comprehensive study of the infrared flux ratios of the [NeV] 14 μm/24 μm and [SIII] 18 μm/33 μm emission lines, which are commonly used to infer the density of ionized gas. Our analysis is based on 41 Type 1 and Type 2 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) observed with Spitzer’s Infrared Spectrograph.

For most galaxies in which both [NeV] lines are detected, the measured [NeV] flux ratios are either compatible with, or fall below, the theoretical low-density limit. This limit is derived from calculations that use the collision strengths currently available and do not account for absorption or stimulated emission. We determine that Type 2 AGNs show smaller line flux ratios than Type 1 AGNs, and every galaxy with a ratio below the low-density limit belongs to the Type 2 class.

We propose that these sub-limit ratios are caused by wavelength-dependent infrared extinction affecting the [NeV]-emitting region, produced by dust in the obscuring torus. We further suggest that the [NeV] ratio could serve as an indicator of the torus inclination relative to our viewing direction. However, because the gas temperature, the degree of extinction, and the influence of absorption and stimulated emission on the ratios are not known, we cannot derive electron densities from the [NeV] flux ratios for the sources in our sample.

We also show that [SIII] emission in these galaxies is spatially extended and arises mainly from star-forming regions. As a result, for most nearby galaxies, analyses based on flux ratios of low-ionization lines are unreliable when the measurements come from slits with different aperture sizes.
outputs.L3:
The study presents a systematic investigation of infrared emission-line flux ratios in a sample of 41 Type 1 and Type 2 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) observed with the Infrared Spectrograph aboard the *Spitzer Space Telescope*. In particular, it focuses on the [Ne V] and [S III] fine-structure lines, which are useful diagnostics of the physical conditions and geometry of the emitting regions in active galaxies.

For the [Ne V] emission, the authors examine galaxies in which both infrared [Ne V] lines are detected. They find that most of these objects have line flux ratios that are either consistent with, or fall below, the theoretical low-density limit. This is significant because, under standard assumptions, line ratios below this limit are not expected from simple density effects alone. The result therefore suggests that additional physical processes must be influencing the observed line strengths.

A clear difference is found between Type 1 and Type 2 AGNs. Type 2 AGNs tend to show lower [Ne V] line flux ratios than Type 1 AGNs, and every galaxy with a ratio below the theoretical low-density limit belongs to the Type 2 class. This pattern points to a connection between the observed [Ne V] ratios and the orientation-dependent obscuration that distinguishes the two AGN types.

The authors argue that the most plausible explanation for the unusually low [Ne V] ratios is differential infrared extinction caused by dust in the obscuring torus surrounding the active nucleus. Because the two [Ne V] lines occur at different infrared wavelengths, dust can attenuate them by different amounts, altering the observed ratio. In this interpretation, lower [Ne V] ratios indicate stronger obscuration and may therefore provide a way to trace the inclination angle of the torus relative to the observer’s line of sight.

The study also considers [S III] emission, but finds that it behaves differently from [Ne V]. The [S III] lines are spatially extended and arise primarily in star-forming regions rather than in the compact narrow-line region close to the AGN. As a result, analyses that rely on low-ionization infrared line ratios measured through different slit sizes are generally unreliable for most nearby galaxies. Since the emitting region is extended, different apertures can sample different fractions of the total [S III] emission, producing misleading ratios that do not accurately reflect the intrinsic physical conditions of the gas.
outputs.L4:
A systematic study using archival and published observations from the *Spitzer* Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) examined mid-infrared fine-structure emission lines in a sample of 41 active galactic nuclei (AGNs), including both Type 1 and Type 2 objects. The main goal was to test whether selected infrared line-flux ratios can be used as reliable diagnostics of the density and structure of ionized gas in AGNs. In particular, the study focused on the high-ionization [Ne V] emission lines and the lower-ionization [S III] lines, both of which arise in ionized gas but trace different physical regions.

The [Ne V] lines are especially useful for studying AGNs because they require very high ionization energies and are therefore closely associated with the active nucleus rather than with normal star-forming regions. The ratio of the [Ne V] 14.3 μm and 24.3 μm lines can, in principle, be used as an electron-density diagnostic for gas in the narrow-line region. However, the study found a systematic difference between AGN types: Type 2 AGNs tend to show lower [Ne V] 14.3 μm/24.3 μm flux ratios than Type 1 AGNs. In many Type 2 objects, the measured ratios fall below the theoretical low-density limit expected from standard atomic physics calculations.

Because line ratios below the low-density limit cannot be explained simply by ordinary changes in gas density, the result suggests that another effect is altering the observed fluxes. The most likely explanation is differential extinction by dust associated with the obscuring torus in AGNs. In the unified model of AGNs, Type 1 objects are viewed more directly, while Type 2 objects are seen at higher inclination, with the central region partly hidden by dusty material. Since the 14.3 μm and 24.3 μm lines are affected differently by mid-infrared extinction, obscuration by the torus can suppress one line relative to the other and drive the observed [Ne V] ratio below its intrinsic value. The lower ratios observed in Type 2 AGNs therefore provide evidence that even mid-infrared high-ionization lines can be affected by orientation-dependent extinction.

The study also considered the [S III] 18.7 μm and 33.5 μm lines, which are commonly used as density diagnostics for lower-ionization gas. However, these lines are more problematic in AGNs because [S III] emission can arise not only from the narrow-line region but also from extended star-forming regions in the host galaxy. In addition, the two [S III] lines were observed with different IRS slit sizes. The 33.5 μm line is measured with a larger aperture than the 18.7 μm line, meaning that it can include more extended emission from the host galaxy. As a result, the observed [S III] 18.7 μm/33.5 μm ratio may be strongly affected by aperture mismatch rather than by the true density of the gas.

This aperture effect makes the [S III] ratio unreliable as a straightforward density diagnostic in many AGNs, especially when the low-ionization emission is spatially extended. If additional [S III] flux from star-forming regions enters the larger slit, the 33.5 μm line can be artificially enhanced, lowering the measured ratio and producing misleading density estimates. Thus, while [Ne V] provides a more direct probe of the AGN narrow-line region, its ratios must still be interpreted with caution because of possible torus extinction and inclination effects. Conversely, [S III] ratios are particularly vulnerable to contamination by extended host-galaxy emission and differences in instrumental aperture.

Overall, the study shows that mid-infrared fine-structure lines are valuable tools for probing the physical conditions in AGNs, but their interpretation requires careful attention to geometry, extinction, and aperture effects. The systematically lower [Ne V] ratios in Type 2 AGNs support the idea that orientation and dusty obscuration influence even infrared emission-line measurements. At the same time, the behavior of the [S III] ratios demonstrates that low-ionization infrared lines can be significantly contaminated by star formation and extended galactic emission. Reliable density measurements therefore require both appropriate line selection and careful correction for observational and structural effects.
outputs.L5:
NeV, SIII, and Type classifications are important terms in astrophysical spectroscopy, especially when studying ionized gas in galaxies, nebulae, and active galactic nuclei.

NeV refers to highly ionized neon, often written as [Ne V] in spectral analysis. Its presence usually indicates very energetic radiation, because producing NeV requires photons with high ionization energy. For this reason, [Ne V] emission is commonly associated with active galactic nuclei or other extreme environments where powerful sources of radiation are present.

SIII, or [S III], represents doubly ionized sulfur. This emission is often detected in ionized gas regions such as H II regions, star-forming galaxies, and planetary nebulae. Compared with NeV, SIII traces less extreme ionization conditions and is useful for measuring the physical properties of gas, such as density, temperature, and chemical abundance.

The word Type can refer to different classification systems depending on the context. In astronomy, objects may be classified by Type based on their spectra, ionization level, morphology, or activity. For example, galaxies may be described as star-forming, composite, or active depending on emission-line ratios, while supernovae are classified into Types such as Type Ia, Type Ib, Type Ic, and Type II.

Together, NeV, SIII, and Type help scientists interpret the nature of astronomical objects. The detection of [Ne V] can suggest a hard radiation source, [S III] can reveal conditions in ionized gas, and Type classification provides a framework for comparing objects and understanding their physical origin.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for an astronomy paper analyzing Spitzer IRS [NeV] 14/24 micron and [SIII] 18/33 micron infrared line flux ratios in 41 Type 1 and Type 2 AGNs, focusing on density diagnostics, low-density-limit issues, extinction by the torus, and extended star-formation contamination.
counterfactuals.output:
We present an analysis of mid-infrared density-sensitive fine-structure line ratios in a sample of 41 nearby Type 1 and Type 2 active galactic nuclei observed with the *Spitzer* Infrared Spectrograph. We examine the [Ne V] 14.32/24.32 μm and [S III] 18.71/33.48 μm flux ratios as diagnostics of the electron density in the narrow-line region and circumnuclear gas, with particular attention to systematic effects that can drive the observed ratios below their theoretical low-density limits. The [Ne V] ratio, arising from highly ionized gas associated primarily with the AGN, frequently yields values consistent with low-density narrow-line region gas, but a significant fraction of objects—especially Type 2 AGNs—show depressed 14/24 μm ratios. We interpret these low ratios as evidence for differential mid-infrared extinction by dusty material, plausibly associated with the obscuring torus or compact circumnuclear dust, rather than as a true density effect. The implied extinction is modest in the mid-infrared but can be substantial at optical wavelengths, consistent with unified models in which the high-ionization line-emitting region is viewed through larger columns in Type 2 sources.

In contrast, the [S III] 18/33 μm ratio, which traces lower-ionization gas and is more susceptible to host-galaxy emission, shows a broader range of behavior and is more often affected by aperture and contamination effects. Because the 33 μm line is measured with a larger IRS aperture than the 18 μm line, extended star formation can enhance the long-wavelength flux and artificially lower the observed [S III] ratio, in some cases pushing it below the nominal low-density limit. We find that such contamination is most important in objects with strong polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission or other indicators of circumnuclear star formation. After accounting qualitatively for extinction and aperture-dependent extended emission, most line ratios are consistent with electron densities in the low- to moderate-density regime expected for AGN narrow-line regions and star-forming gas.

Our results demonstrate that mid-infrared fine-structure ratios provide valuable density constraints in AGNs, but their interpretation requires careful treatment of low-density-limit violations, wavelength-dependent extinction, and spatially extended host-galaxy emission. The [Ne V] 14/24 μm ratio is a particularly useful probe of obscuration toward the inner narrow-line region, while the [S III] 18/33 μm ratio is more strongly influenced by star-formation contamination and IRS aperture mismatches. These diagnostics therefore offer complementary constraints on the structure of dusty AGN environments and the relative contributions of nuclear and host-galaxy gas in infrared spectroscopic observations.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main findings of a study of [NeV] and [SIII] mid-infrared emission line ratios in nearby active galactic nuclei observed with Spitzer, including differences between Type 1 and Type 2 AGNs and implications for using these ratios as electron density indicators.
counterfactuals.output:
A Spitzer/IRS study of nearby active galactic nuclei used the mid-infrared fine-structure ratios

- **[Ne V] 14.3 μm / 24.3 μm**  
- **[S III] 18.7 μm / 33.5 μm**

to test their usefulness as electron-density diagnostics in AGN narrow-line regions.

Main findings:

- **[Ne V] ratios differ between AGN types.**  
  Type 1 AGNs generally show **higher [Ne V] 14/24 ratios** than Type 2 AGNs. Because [Ne V] is a high-ionization line arising close to the AGN, this difference is likely connected to nuclear geometry and obscuration.

- **Many Type 2 AGNs have unusually low [Ne V] ratios.**  
  Several observed [Ne V] 14/24 ratios fall near or even below the theoretical low-density limit. Such values cannot be straightforwardly interpreted as very low electron densities. Instead, they may reflect:
  - differential dust extinction, especially stronger attenuation of the 14.3 μm line,
  - silicate absorption effects,
  - aperture mismatches between the IRS short- and long-wavelength modules,
  - or uncertainties in atomic data/calibration.

- **The [Ne V] ratio is therefore not a simple density indicator in obscured AGNs.**  
  In principle, [Ne V] 14/24 is sensitive to electron density in the narrow-line region, but in practice the ratio can be strongly affected by extinction and geometry. For Type 2 sources in particular, a low [Ne V] ratio should not automatically be converted into a low density.

- **[S III] ratios show weaker or no clear Type 1/Type 2 separation.**  
  [S III] traces lower-ionization gas, often more extended and more easily contaminated by star-forming regions in the host galaxy. Its emission is less uniquely tied to the AGN narrow-line region.

- **[S III] is especially vulnerable to aperture effects.**  
  The 18.7 μm and 33.5 μm lines were observed with different Spitzer IRS apertures. Since [S III] emission can be spatially extended, the larger aperture at 33.5 μm can collect more flux, artificially lowering the 18.7/33.5 ratio. This can push observed ratios below the nominal low-density limit.

- **Implication for density measurements:**  
  Both ratios must be used cautiously. The **[Ne V] ratio is potentially useful for compact, high-ionization AGN gas**, but obscuration and extinction can bias it, especially in Type 2 AGNs. The **[S III] ratio is less reliable as an AGN narrow-line density probe** unless aperture effects and host-galaxy/star-formation contamination are carefully corrected.

Overall, the study found that mid-infrared line ratios are valuable diagnostics, but their interpretation is not purely a matter of electron density. AGN orientation, dust obscuration, spatial extent of the emitting gas, and instrumental aperture differences all play major roles.

counterfactuals.output: We present a systematic analysis of the mid-infrared fine-structure line flux ratios [Ne V] 14.3 μm/24.3 μm and [S III] 18.7 μm/33.5 μm in a 41-object sample of active galactic nuclei observed with the *Spitzer* Infrared Spectrograph. These ratios provide complementary probes of electron density in highly ionized narrow-line gas and lower-ionization circumnuclear material, respectively, while being relatively insensitive to gas temperature. We measure line fluxes uniformly from low- and high-resolution IRS spectra and examine the effects of instrumental aperture mismatch, blending, continuum placement, and mid-infrared extinction. The observed [Ne V] and [S III] ratios span a broad range, with many sources lying near the theoretical low-density limits and a subset exhibiting elevated ratios indicative of denser emitting regions. Comparison with atomic excitation models suggests that the [Ne V]-emitting gas typically traces higher-ionization, compact narrow-line regions, whereas [S III] often includes a more extended contribution from lower-density gas associated with the host galaxy or star-forming regions. Deviations from expected ratios can be explained by a combination of density structure, differential extinction, and aperture-related systematics. This study demonstrates the diagnostic power of mid-infrared line ratios for characterizing the physical conditions of AGN narrow-line regions and highlights the need for careful treatment of observational systematics when interpreting unresolved infrared spectroscopy.

counterfactuals.output:
### Abstract / Conclusion Draft

We present an analysis of mid-infrared fine-structure line ratios in a sample of active galactic nuclei (AGNs), focusing on the density-sensitive [Ne V] and [S III] diagnostics. A significant fraction of the AGNs exhibit [Ne V] infrared line ratios at, or even below, the theoretical low-density limit. This behavior is most pronounced among Type 2 sources, suggesting that the observed ratios are not primarily driven by unusually low gas densities or atomic-physics uncertainties, but instead by differential dust extinction affecting the [Ne V]-emitting narrow-line region. In particular, obscuration by the dusty torus can preferentially attenuate the shorter-wavelength [Ne V] line, lowering the observed ratio and producing values inconsistent with simple optically thin low-density expectations.

In contrast, the [S III] emission shows evidence for a different physical origin. Its line ratios and spatial behavior indicate that the [S III]-emitting gas is more extended than the high-ionization [Ne V] region and is often dominated by star-forming regions in the host galaxy rather than by the AGN narrow-line region alone. This distinction highlights the importance of separating compact, high-ionization AGN tracers from lower-ionization emission that may include substantial host-galaxy contamination.

Overall, our results demonstrate that mid-infrared line ratios in AGNs cannot always be interpreted as straightforward density diagnostics without accounting for geometry, extinction, and the spatial distribution of the emitting gas. The prevalence of anomalously low [Ne V] ratios, especially in obscured AGNs, provides evidence that dust in the torus or inner narrow-line region significantly modifies the observed mid-infrared spectrum. Meanwhile, the extended nature of [S III] emission underscores the role of star formation in shaping lower-ionization infrared diagnostics. These findings support a picture in which high-ionization mid-infrared lines trace the obscured AGN environment, while lower-ionization species often reflect a composite of AGN and host-galaxy processes.

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal astrophysics journal style, describe a study using mid-infrared fine-structure line ratios from Spitzer IRS spectra to test electron density diagnostics in Type 1 and Type 2 AGNs, discussing [NeV], [SIII], torus inclination, extinction, and slit-size limitations.
counterfactuals.output:
We present a mid-infrared spectroscopic investigation of electron-density diagnostics in active galactic nuclei (AGNs), based on fine-structure line ratios measured from archival *Spitzer* Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) observations of Type 1 and Type 2 sources. The principal density-sensitive diagnostics considered are the [Ne V] 14.32 μm/24.32 μm and [S III] 18.71 μm/33.48 μm flux ratios, which probe highly ionized narrow-line gas and lower-ionization circumnuclear gas, respectively. Because the [Ne V] transitions arise from an ionization potential of 97.1 eV, they provide a relatively clean diagnostic of AGN-photoionized material, whereas [S III] can include contributions from both the narrow-line region and circumnuclear star-forming regions.

The observed [Ne V] ratios are compared with theoretical predictions computed for a range of electron densities and temperatures using standard atomic collision strengths and transition probabilities. In the low-density limit, the [Ne V] 14 μm/24 μm ratio approaches a nearly temperature-insensitive asymptotic value, while at densities approaching or exceeding the critical densities of the transitions the ratio increases. The measured ratios for both Type 1 and Type 2 AGNs are generally consistent with low to moderate narrow-line-region densities, although a subset of objects exhibits ratios below the nominal theoretical low-density limit. Such low ratios are unlikely to be explained by density effects alone and instead indicate the importance of observational and radiative-transfer systematics, including differential extinction, aperture mismatches, flux calibration uncertainties, and possible spatial stratification of the emitting gas.

A key objective of the study is to test whether the mid-infrared density diagnostics reveal systematic differences between optical AGN classes. In the simplest orientation-based unification scenario, Type 1 and Type 2 AGNs differ primarily by the inclination of an obscuring dusty torus relative to the line of sight. If the mid-infrared narrow-line emission were isotropic and unaffected by obscuration, the [Ne V] and [S III] ratios would be expected to show no strong dependence on optical type. Conversely, if the torus or associated dusty structures obscure part of the inner narrow-line region, Type 2 AGNs could display altered line ratios, particularly for diagnostics involving transitions separated significantly in wavelength. The comparison shows that Type 1 and Type 2 objects occupy broadly overlapping regions in line-ratio space, suggesting that the mid-infrared fine-structure ratios are not dominated by orientation effects alone. However, modest differences in the distributions cannot be excluded, especially in sources with strong silicate absorption or evidence for compact, heavily embedded nuclear emission.

The [Ne V] 14.32 μm/24.32 μm ratio is particularly sensitive to extinction because the two lines lie on opposite sides of the 18 μm silicate feature and can be differently affected by dust absorption. For a foreground-screen geometry, extinction tends to suppress the shorter-wavelength 14 μm line more strongly than the 24 μm line, thereby lowering the observed ratio. In more realistic mixed or clumpy geometries, the effect can be more complex, depending on the relative locations of the [Ne V]-emitting gas and the obscuring dust. The presence of anomalously low [Ne V] ratios in some objects is therefore plausibly associated with mid-infrared extinction, especially in inclined or dust-rich systems. Nevertheless, the absence of a one-to-one correspondence between optical class and depressed [Ne V] ratio implies that torus inclination is not the only controlling parameter; host-galaxy dust lanes, circumnuclear star formation, and the radial distribution of ionized gas may also be important.

The [S III] 18.71 μm/33.48 μm ratio provides an independent density probe at lower ionization. In many objects this ratio indicates electron densities comparable to, or lower than, those inferred from [Ne V], although interpretation is complicated by the larger spatial extent of [S III] emission. Star-forming regions in the host galaxy can contribute significantly to the [S III] flux, particularly in large IRS apertures. As a result, the [S III] ratio may not trace the same gas component as [Ne V]. Discrepancies between the two diagnostics are therefore interpreted as evidence for ionization and density stratification, aperture-dependent contamination, or both, rather than as failures of the atomic density diagnostics themselves.

A significant limitation of the analysis arises from the differing IRS slit sizes used for the relevant transitions. The [Ne V] 14.32 μm and [S III] 18.71 μm lines are observed in the Short-High module, whereas [Ne V] 24.32 μm and [S III] 33.48 μm are observed in the Long-High module. The Long-High slit subtends a substantially larger area on the sky, so extended emission can enhance the longer-wavelength line fluxes relative to the shorter-wavelength measurements. This aperture mismatch can artificially depress the 14/24 and 18/33 ratios, mimicking the effect of lower density or increased extinction. The problem is most severe for nearby or spatially extended galaxies, for which the narrow-line region and circumnuclear star-forming structures are partially resolved by *Spitzer*. Consequently, ratios lying below theoretical low-density limits should not be interpreted solely in terms of electron density without careful consideration of source extent and slit geometry.

Overall, the study demonstrates that mid-infrared fine-structure line ratios remain valuable probes of AGN narrow-line-region density, but their diagnostic power is limited by extinction, aperture effects, and the complex spatial structure of the emitting gas. The [Ne V] ratio is the most direct AGN density indicator, while [S III] provides complementary information on lower-ionization gas and possible host-galaxy contamination. The broadly similar line-ratio distributions of Type 1 and Type 2 AGNs are broadly consistent with orientation-based unification, but the observed scatter and the presence of sub-theoretical ratios indicate that torus inclination, mid-infrared extinction, and slit-size effects must all be included in any quantitative interpretation. Future high-angular-resolution mid-infrared spectroscopy with matched apertures will be essential for isolating the compact narrow-line region and for establishing robust electron-density diagnostics across AGN subclasses.
